evidence.text:
# R001 experiment design: November free-agent pool triage (MILBFA)

Status: DRAFT v1, written 2026-10-09 before any outcome labels were inspected. Pending the early independent challenge (section 12). Changes after the challenge are recorded as v2 with reasons; this v1 stays as written.

## Decision and user

- User: a club's pro scouting director and the front-office staff who decide minor-league contracts and non-roster invitations (NRIs).
- Recurring decision: every November, several hundred players elect free agency within days (S1: 585 to 908 "elected free agency" events per Nov-Dec window, 2018-2025). Staff must decide which few to pursue and in what order, with limited scouting attention.
- Intervention: a ranked list of the whole pool, built only from public information available on the decision date, with each player's evidence shown.

## Hypothesis (falsifiable)

H1: Ranking the November pool by a simple public-data model puts more next-season MLB contributors in the top k than a naive baseline ranking does.

- Population: every player with an "elected free agency" transaction (type DFA, description text "elected free agency") dated Nov 1 to Dec 31 of season Y. This avoids S1's unresolved minor-league vs MLB separation: the decision-maker sees the whole pool. A decision-time stratifier is reported separately: "no MLB appearance in season Y" (the low-attention segment), derived from season-Y stats.
- Outcome (binary, defined now): the player records at least 50 MLB plate appearances or at least 20 MLB innings pitched in season Y+1, for any club. Secondary: any MLB appearance in Y+1.
- Features: only data with event time and availability time no later than Dec 31 of season Y: age at Dec 31, highest level reached in Y, season-Y stats by level (rate stats and playing time), MLB playing time in Y and Y-1, position group (pitcher / hitter). No later transactions, no Y+1 data, no projections published after the decision date.

## Baselines (simple, comparable information)

- B0 (naive experience): rank by MLB playing time in season Y, then highest level reached, then younger first.
- B1 (simple rule a scout might use): rank by highest level reached in Y, then a level-appropriate rate stat (OPS for hitters, K-BB% for pitchers), then age.
- Model M: logistic regression on the features above, fitted on training cohorts only, preprocessing fitted on training data only. No hyperparameter search beyond a fixed, recorded regularization choice tuned on the validation cohort.

## Splits and holdout

- Training cohorts: 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 (outcome seasons 2019, 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024). There is no 2020 cohort (no minor-league season in 2020). The 2019 cohort's outcome season is 2020 (shortened season): the outcome threshold is scaled by games played (60/162) and the cohort is also reported excluded as a sensitivity check.
- Validation cohort: 2024 (outcomes 2025), used once for the fixed regularization choice and for comparing M against B0/B1 during development.
- Final holdout: 2025 cohort (outcomes 2026, a season already complete on 2026-10-09). Not inspected for outcomes before the final evaluation. As of this writing the 2025 cohort's pool size is known from S1 (839 events), but no 2026 outcome has been retrieved or looked at.
- Players appear in multiple cohorts; the split is by cohort year (temporal), and the same player in different years is treated as separate decisions. Reported: how many holdout players also appear in training cohorts.

## Primary metric and uncertainty

- Primary: number of outcome-positive players in the top k = 50 of the ranking, holdout cohort, M vs B1 (the stronger simple baseline, chosen as whichever of B0/B1 is better on validation; recorded before holdout).
- Why k = 50: roughly the scale of minor-league contracts plus NRIs a club offers in an offseason (to be checked against public Cubs signings in the Cubs case; if the measured number differs a lot, k is re-justified before the holdout, not after).
- Secondary: precision@25, precision@100, AUROC, calibration of M.
- Uncertainty: paired bootstrap over players in the holdout cohort (2,000 resamples) for the difference in top-50 hits and AUROC; report 95% intervals.

## Practical significance and stopping

- Meaningful improvement: M finds at least 3 more outcome-positive players in its top 50 than the baseline, with the paired bootstrap interval excluding 0. Rationale: with base rates expected to be low, a few extra usable depth players per offseason is the scale at which a pro department's attention would shift; smaller differences are within scout-level noise.
- Rejection: if M does not beat the baseline by that margin on the holdout, the usefulness claim is rejected (COMPLETE_NEGATIVE), and no Cubs recommendation is made from M.
- Stop early (before modelling) if: outcome-positive base rate in training cohorts is so low (< 15 positives per cohort) that top-50 comparisons are not informative; record and use the pivot or stop.

## What this can and cannot establish

- Can: whether public decision-time data ranks the November pool better than simple rules, retrospectively.
- Cannot: causal benefit (outcome depends on opportunity given by the signing club), adoption, wins, or comparison with clubs' private evaluations.
- Known bias: a player's next-season MLB time partly reflects which club signed him and its roster needs.

## Cubs application (dated)

Retrospective case: as of 2025-12-31, apply the frozen method to the 2025 pool, list its top 50 and the "no MLB in 2025" segment, and compare with the minor-league contracts and NRIs the Cubs publicly signed that offseason (public transactions), then with 2026 outcomes. Report what the method would have flagged that the Cubs did not sign and vice versa, without claiming the method would have improved the Cubs' results. If H1 is rejected, the case illustrates limitations only.

## Smallest implementation

A CLI in cubs-edge-lab that builds the cohort tables from the existing probe cache plus the additional public queries it needs (season-Y stats and Y+1 outcomes per player), computes features with explicit as-of dates, fits M on training cohorts, evaluates M/B0/B1 with bootstrap intervals, and writes a dated ranked list for a chosen cohort. Bulk data stays local (MLBAM terms); committed outputs are aggregates and short examples.

## Bounds

HowlPlane sessions remaining for R001: 3 of 12 (user-raised bound). Data acquisition, build, and evaluation must fit; if not, pause and ask.

Measured with the public MLB Stats API (cubs-edge-lab research/FEASIBILITY.md, merged 35f803b). 'Elected free agency' events (typeCode DFA) dated Nov 1 - Dec 31 per offseason: 2018 585, 2019 631, 2021 908, 2022 854, 2023 833, 2024 638, 2025 839. Two methods to separate minor-league from MLB elections disagree (2018: method A 530 minor / 52 MLB / 3 unresolved; method B 417 / 133 / 35). Rule 5 MLB-phase codes R5 appear only from 2024 (15 in Dec 2024). Minor-league dated game logs are returned for sampled players. Source terms: individual, non-commercial, non-bulk use only.

speculative_candidates.objective: Where could software create a meaningful baseball advantage for the Chicago Cubs? Second pass, informed by a critique of earlier ideas. The critique found: (a) most public-data analytics tools reach only parity with sophisticated clubs that hold private tracking, medical and scouting data; (b) earlier ideas were analyst-centric information tools with no named decision owner and no measurable change in decisions; (c) uncovered areas include amateur draft and scouting workflow, pro acquisition, trade and free-agent valuation, contract and non-tender decisions, defense, strength and conditioning, and coordination or error-prevention tools rather than information tools. The current date is in the Cubs' offseason (their 2026 season ended in the Wild Card Series), so prefer decisions that recur every offseason or every season and that can be evaluated retrospectively on public history. Seek mechanisms by which public data could still create an edge despite private-data clubs: speed, coverage of neglected populations, combining signals few look at, market inefficiencies in league-wide processes, or avoiding systematic human biases. Also name where software is unnecessary. OUTPUT GUIDANCE (format only): Each IDEA names one problem, the decision owner, the concrete recurring decision, the mechanism of advantage, and the software intervention. Follow with ASSUMPTION and UNKNOWN lines. Do not invent statistics or private Cubs information.
speculative_candidates.text: IDEA: Problem: minor league free agency each November releases many upper-minors players, and evaluation is often cursory. Owner: pro scouting director and farm director. Decision: minor league free agent signings and spring invites every offseason. Mechanism: coverage of a neglected population, plus speed. Intervention: a prebuilt eligible-player list from public service-time and transaction data, ranked by public Triple-A and Double-A tracking metrics where available, with a one-page profile per player.

assumptions: Public small-conference and summer-league stats are standardized and accurate enough to rank players within those populations.
Rival clubs have not already closed this gap with their own private tracking at summer leagues.
Late-round and undrafted-free-agent outcomes add enough value to justify reallocating scout time.
Pool-rule errors or suboptimal sequencing actually occur often enough to matter, as opposed to being solved by spreadsheets.
Signability information exists in a structured form and can be entered quickly.
Non-tendered players are systematically undervalued, which needs testing against public signing history and subsequent performance.
Early contact materially improves signing odds, as opposed to players waiting for the market.
Anonymization is feasible with publicly known players. Decision makers may recognize statlines.
Sunk-cost bias exists in tender decisions and is measurable retrospectively.
Public roster and eligibility data are complete enough to reconstruct 40-man pressure for all 30 clubs.
Roster-pressured clubs actually accept lower returns, which needs testing on historical trades.
This differs from the explored waiver/DFA monitor because it targets the pre-emptive trade ask rather than the waiver claim.
Profile-specific aging differs enough from generic curves to change offer decisions.
Sample sizes per profile are large enough to avoid overfitting.
Private-data clubs have not already priced this in, which is the critique's parity risk.
Inconsistency actually exists and has measurable cost in defensive outcomes or adjustment time.
Affiliate positioning data is available. Public minor league defensive tracking may be limited.
Adherence is a meaningful bottleneck and is not already handled by existing vendor platforms.
Players and the union would accept the tool. Privacy, health-data, and collective bargaining constraints may apply.
Minor league free agents produce enough major league value retrospectively to justify the effort.
Public eligibility data is reliable.
Counterfactual availability can be reconstructed from public data without knowing private negotiation context.
Outcome noise is not so large that the scorecard just measures luck.
Low-tool areas really are low-value for software, which should be checked against observed errors before dismissing them.

Problem: draft boards may underweight players from neglected populations such as cold-weather high schools, small-conference colleges, and junior colleges, where public coverage is thin. Owner: amateur scouting director. Decision: area-scout coverage allocation and late-round board ordering each spring. Mechanism: coverage of neglected populations, plus correcting the bias toward players who were seen more often. Intervention: a coverage-gap map that compares public box-score and summer-league performance against logged scout looks, flagging high-signal players with few looks.
club_scout_coverage_logs
public_small_conference_data_quality

Problem: draft-day decisions are made under time pressure, and bonus-pool slot math is error-prone. Owner: scouting director with front-office pool manager. Decision: in-draft pick selection and underslot/overslot sequencing each July. Mechanism: speed and error prevention rather than information. Intervention: a live pool-ledger simulator that shows the remaining pool, forfeiture thresholds, and signability-contingent pick sequences, then runs a pre-draft rehearsal against historical draft orders.
historical_frequency_of_pool_sequencing_mistakes_league_wide

Problem: the non-tender deadline produces a league-wide supply shock of freed players, and clubs may evaluate them slowly or anchor on the prior club's judgment. Owner: GM and pro scouting director. Decision: which non-tendered players to pursue, and how fast, every offseason. Mechanism: speed, plus exploiting a market inefficiency in a league-wide process. Intervention: a pre-deadline model, built in October and November, that forecasts likely non-tenders from public salary projections and performance, then pre-ranks them and pre-drafts offer ranges so the club can act within hours.
retrospective_value_of_nontendered_players_vs_contract_cost
typical_signing_speed_after_nontender_deadline

Problem: the club's own non-tender and tender decisions may be biased by sunk cost or familiarity. Owner: GM. Decision: tender or non-tender of arbitration-eligible players each November. Mechanism: avoiding systematic human bias. Intervention: a blinded review in which tender candidates are mixed anonymously with comparable external non-tender candidates, and decision makers price each one without names before a decision journal records the final call.
evidence_of_endowment_bias_in_mlb_tender_decisions

Problem: trade negotiations may focus on headline players while undervaluing low-minors throw-ins and players blocked by a full 40-man roster elsewhere. Owner: GM and pro scouting director. Decision: which secondary pieces to request in each trade, and which Rule 5-eligible players other clubs must protect or expose, every winter. Mechanism: market inefficiency in league-wide roster-crunch processes, plus combining signals. Intervention: a league-wide 40-man pressure map built from public transaction and roster data that flags clubs forced to shed players before Rule 5 protection and offseason deadlines, and suggests targeted asks.
historical_trade_return_vs_counterparty_roster_pressure

Problem: free-agent contract valuations may misprice aging curves for specific skill profiles, such as speed-dependent or defense-first players. Owner: GM and front-office valuation group. Decision: offer years and dollars to free agents each winter. Mechanism: combining signals few weigh together, specifically public sprint speed trends, defensive metrics, and contract outcomes. Intervention: a skill-profile-specific aging model that is backtested only on public contracts and shows retrospective error bands against the generic aging assumption.
public_contract_outcome_dataset_completeness

Problem: defensive alignment and positioning across the minor league system may be inconsistent with major league standards, so players arrive needing to relearn positioning. Owner: player development director and field coordinators. Decision: each season's standardized defensive positioning conventions and communication signs across affiliates. Mechanism: coordination and error prevention, not information. Intervention: a shared positioning-card generator plus a compliance check that compares affiliate conventions to major league conventions and flags divergences.
affiliate_defensive_positioning_data_availability

Problem: the offseason strength and conditioning programs of remote players are hard to monitor and coordinate, especially across languages and locations. Owner: head of strength and conditioning. Decision: individualized offseason program assignment and check-ins each winter. Mechanism: coordination, plus catching non-adherence early. Intervention: a lightweight check-in and program-versioning tool with player consent and minimal data collection. It is not an information tool but a reminder and adherence ledger.
existing_vendor_platform_adoption_by_club
cba_constraints_on_offseason_monitoring

Problem: minor league free agency each November releases many upper-minors players, and evaluation is often cursory. Owner: pro scouting director and farm director. Decision: minor league free agent signings and spring invites every offseason. Mechanism: coverage of a neglected population, plus speed. Intervention: a prebuilt eligible-player list from public service-time and transaction data, ranked by public Triple-A and Double-A tracking metrics where available, with a one-page profile per player.
retrospective_mlb_value_of_minor_league_free_agents

Problem: the club cannot tell whether its offseason decision processes beat the market. Owner: GM and front-office leadership. Decision: an annual process audit each October. Mechanism: retrospective evaluation on public history, which ties software to measurable decision changes. Intervention: a scorecard that compares each offseason's acquisitions, non-tenders, and passes against the counterfactual of players available but not chosen, using public outcomes.
club_decision_records_for_counterfactual_matching
Where software is unnecessary: relationship-driven decisions such as player recruitment pitches, clubhouse fit judgments, and agent rapport gain little from new software beyond basic notes.
Where software is unnecessary: one-off contract structure creativity, such as opt-outs and deferrals, mostly needs human negotiation. A simple present-value calculator already suffices.
Where software is unnecessary: if a decision recurs rarely and the existing spreadsheet error rate is near zero, building a tool adds maintenance cost without an edge.
